interactions.summary: Jiang pushes the class to place Virgil inside Dante's moral universe, where several students conclude he belongs among the worst traitors, and the class then starts exploring why Dante or Beatrice might still suspend that judgment.

claims.claim: Jiang rejects the idea that creativity itself excuses Virgil, saying conscious misuse of the gift makes his betrayal worse, not better.
Within Dante's moral framework, Jiang says Virgil belongs at the very bottom of hell among the great betrayers, even worse than Lucifer in some respects.
A student counters that Dante may keep Virgil in Limbo out of love or forgiveness, because Dante cannot imagine himself without Virgil as precursor.
Another student suggests Virgil may have been temporarily moved or disguised by heavenly powers for Dante's sake, even if his true station is worse.

signature_moments.moment: Jiang imagines Virgil not as a noble pagan but as someone who ought to be in Lucifer's mouth for condemning Europe to centuries of merciless empire.
signature_moments.source_phrase: it's the iniad that has condemned europe to a thousand years of hell
signature_moments.why_it_matters: It makes the anti-Virgil reading historically explosive rather than merely literary.

chronology_notes.note: The class now treats Virgil's Limbo status itself as suspicious, requiring either Dantean mercy or a heavenly reprieve to explain why a great betrayer is not visibly damned.
